desc:
A string has been compressed with run-length encoding: every run of equal letters was replaced by the letter followed by the length of the run written in decimal. For example, "aaabcc" became "a3b1c2".

Given the encoded string s, return the original string. The encoding is always well formed: it alternates a lowercase letter and a positive number (without leading zeros). The same letter may appear in two neighbouring groups, as in "a2a1", which decodes to "aaa".

s = "a3b1c2"
result = "aaabcc"

s = "x12y1"
result = "xxxxxxxxxxxxy"
constraints: s is a sequence of groups: one lowercase letter followed by a count with no leading zeros
Every count is at least 1, and the decoded string has at most 40,000 characters
hints: Walk through the string from left to right. A group always starts with a letter.
After reading a letter, keep reading characters while they are digits. The counts can have several digits, such as 12 or 405.
Convert the digit characters to an integer c, append letter * c to a list of pieces, and join the pieces once at the end.
editorial: Scan with an index. At a letter, remember it and advance while the next characters are digits, then convert that digit substring to an integer. Repeat the letter that many times. Because a count may span several digits, you cannot simply read one digit after each letter.

Appending every piece to a list and joining once keeps the total work linear in the size of the input plus the output, O(n + m) time and O(m) space, where m is the decoded length. Repeated string concatenation in a loop is a classic way to turn this into quadratic time in some languages.
